OECDscaleup

OECDscaleup builds the firm-level “high-growth firm” (HGF) / scale-up indicators used in the OECD Scale Up project from confidential national firm microdata, and produces the disclosure-checked aggregate tabulations (characteristics, transitions/evolutions, contribution, predictors) shared back with the OECD. It also runs the OECD trade package (firm-level trade in goods: exporters, importers, exporting scalers) and a new analysis, not part of the Stata packages: the fastest-growing scalers, and scalers that grow into mid-caps.

It is a translation of the OECD’s original Stata packages: the “Second Package” (MASTER_OECD_p2.do and its 5 worker .do files, version 1.3) and the trade package (MASTER_OECD_trade.do, version 1.0). The changelog lists every departure from the Stata code and why.

Installation

The package is not on CRAN. Install it from GitHub with devtools:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("amannj/OECDscaleup", build_vignettes = TRUE)

This installs the default branch (see “Versions” below); add ref = "<branch or tag>" for another version. The package uses renv to pin its dependency versions (renv.lock); run renv::restore() after cloning the repository if you develop on it.

Usage 

library(OECDscaleup)

cfg <- config_scaleup(
  country = "FR",
  input_dir = "path/to/input",   # base_financials_FR.dta, etc.
  output_dir = "path/to/output",
  nace_revision = "2"            # the NACE revision of the sector codes: "2" or "2.1"
)

# checks the input files against the variable dictionary (counts only)
check_inputs(cfg)

# reads the raw .dta inputs, runs the full pipeline, writes every output CSV
outputs <- run_scaleup_pipeline(cfg)

# the trade package (needs trade_RAW_FR.dta as well)
trade_outputs <- run_trade_pipeline(cfg)

# the scaler analysis (top scalers, scalers to mid-caps), from the indicators panel
scaler_outputs <- run_scaler_analysis(cfg)

Every stage is also a pure function (data frames in, data frames out):

accounts_indicators <- build_accounts_indicators(cfg, base_financials)
characteristics     <- compute_characteristics(cfg, accounts_indicators)
persistence         <- compute_persistence(cfg, accounts_indicators)
contribution        <- compute_contribution(cfg, accounts_indicators)
predictors          <- compute_predictors(cfg, accounts_indicators)

See the getting-started article for a worked example with synthetic data, including the dominance confidentiality statistics.

Firm-level microdata is confidential and never leaves the country whose national statistical institute holds it, so no real data ships with this package. Every input variable is documented in the articles Input data and Input data for the trade package, and in the package dataset variable_dictionary.

Verification against the Stata code

The R output was compared table by table with the original Stata code (run in Stata 19.5):

  • Second Package: 9 synthetic scenarios built to reach every branch (country-specific rescaling, exchange rates and region aggregation, optional variables, short panels, dominance statistics, …) and three national firm-level panels (confidential);
  • trade package: 6 synthetic scenarios, 2 cases where Stata stops, and one national trade dataset (confidential).

All output tables match: rows, keys, labels and counts exactly, other values within a relative 1e-4. The comparison harness lives outside this repository, alongside the original Stata code.

Versions

  • Tags stata-parity-v1_3, stata-parity-v1_3-1 (branch master) and trade-parity-v1_0: the R code reproduces the Stata code including its bugs, for verification.
  • Branch FixStataBugs: the bugs fixed (listed one by one in the changelog), the NACE revision and money unit declared in config_scaleup(), the input checks, and a performance pass: a panel of 8 million firm-years runs in about 15 minutes with under 20 GB of memory. Reducing the memory further is planned.
  • Branch ScalerAnalysis (the default branch): everything in FixStataBugs, plus the scaler analysis (compute_top_scalers(), compute_midcap_transitions(), run_scaler_analysis()). It outputs every variant and fallback (cut-offs, indices, mid-cap definitions, coverage diagnostics), so the choice among them is left to the analysis.
